titre: Cecilia Payne, the Hydrogen in Stars, and a Sentence of Caution
accroche: In 1925, Cecilia Payne concludes that stars are mostly hydrogen. Her printed thesis adds that this result is “almost certainly not real.”
contenu_vulgarise:
Open an astronomy book from the early 1920s: stars differ in their composition. In the Sun's spectrum, you can pick out iron, calcium, magnesium. In that of some hot stars, you see mostly helium. In others, hydrogen. The accepted idea is simple: if the lines change, the matter changes. The Sun would be made of materials close to those of Earth.

In 1925, Cecilia Payne defends a thesis at Radcliffe College, at Harvard, that overturns this reading. She is the first to earn a doctorate in astronomy at that institution.

## What the strength of a line doesn't tell you

A spectral line depends on two things: the quantity of an element, and the state of its atoms. At high temperature, atoms lose electrons, which is called ionization, and the line you were observing disappears, without the element having disappeared. Payne applies the ionization theory of the Indian physicist Meghnad Saha to the spectra of the Harvard Observatory. She associates each class of star with a temperature.

The result is that the differences in spectra come mainly from temperature, not composition. Stars have roughly the same ingredients. And those ingredients, according to her calculations, are first and foremost hydrogen and helium. Hydrogen, according to her calculations, dominates by a wide margin.

## “Almost certainly not real”

Henry Norris Russell, a leading figure of American astrophysics and a member of her committee, advises her against arguing that the Sun is mostly hydrogen, and will later call her conclusions “spurious,” because they contradicted the accepted idea that the Sun and the Earth have similar compositions. The idea that the Sun is mostly hydrogen contradicts the consensus. Payne then adds a reservation to the printed thesis: the enormous abundance obtained for hydrogen and helium is “almost certainly not real.”

She holds the right conclusion, then disowns it before authority.

Four years later, in 1929, Russell publishes a very similar result by another method. He cites Payne in a single sentence: hers is “the most important” earlier determination. Yet it is mostly his name that people remember.

## An erasure, but not a total one

The common version says Payne was erased. That is a bit too simple: Russell cites her, and her thesis states the conclusion in black and white as early as 1925. But the credit went to the one whose authority was already established.

That is where the shift lies: an unexpected result did not win acceptance because it was correct, but because a recognized specialist redid it by another route. Being right was not enough; confirmation did the rest.

How many correct results have received, on first pass, a sentence of caution that was not their own?

repere.texte: In the printed 1925 thesis, Payne writes that the enormous abundance obtained for hydrogen and helium in the stellar atmosphere is “almost certainly not real.” Russell, who had opposed it, finds similar values in 1929.

carte.punch: She found what stars are made of, then disowned it in her own thesis.
carte.idee: In 1925, Cecilia Payne shows that the spectra of stars differ by temperature, not by composition, and that hydrogen dominates. Faced with Russell's objection, she adds that this result is “almost certainly not real.” He will find it again in 1929.

quiz.question: Why does Payne conclude that stars with different spectra can have the same composition?
choix: Because the strength of the lines depends mainly on temperature, which ionizes the atoms
Because all the stars in her collection were the same color
Because she analyzed the spectra of a single star, the Sun
Because hydrogen lines are always the weakest
quiz.explication: At high temperature, atoms ionize and their lines change without the element disappearing. Spectra therefore differ mainly by temperature. The other answers do not describe her reasoning.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What sentence does Payne add to her printed 1925 thesis?
choix: That hydrogen is found only in the Sun
That her calculations had to be redone by Russell
That the abundance found for hydrogen and helium is almost certainly not real
That the spectra of the Sun are those of the Earth
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Faced with Russell's objection, she adds that the enormous abundance derived for hydrogen and helium is “almost certainly not real.” The other sentences do not appear there.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Russell do in 1929?
choix: He withdraws his criticism without publishing a result
He refuses to acknowledge the thesis result
He takes Payne's thesis word for word without citing it
He publishes a similar result by another method and cites Payne in one sentence
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In 1929, by another method, Russell arrives at a close result, and notes that Payne's determination is the most important of the earlier ones. So he neither copied her without citing her nor ignored her.
